After Registration: 4 Enforcement Routes in China (AMR, Customs, Platforms, Courts)

Registration gives you standing. Enforcement comes from four separate channels — market regulators, Customs, e-commerce platforms and the courts — each with different prerequisites and different outputs.

One Right, Four Channels

A CNIPA registration is a precondition for almost every enforcement action in China: platform complaint systems, Customs recordal and administrative complaints all ask for the Chinese registration certificate or a recorded licence. An overseas registration, a pending application or a distributor's authorisation letter does not substitute for it.

RouteBest forPrerequisiteTypical output
Administrative (AMR)Clear-cut counterfeits in physical markets, local factories and wholesale stallsRegistration certificate, evidence, complaint drafted in ChineseInspection, seizure, administrative penalty; generally faster and cheaper than litigation
China Customs (GACC)Counterfeit imports/exports, OEM leakage, unauthorised cross-border shipmentsRecordal of the registered mark with the General Administration of CustomsEx officio detention of suspect shipments and notice to the rights holder
Platform IPPInfringing listings on e-commerce and social-commerce platformsBrand enrolment with a CNIPA certificate or a recorded licenceListing removal, repeat-infringer sanctions; reactive, requires your own monitoring
Civil litigationHigh-value, repeat or contested infringement; damages and precedentNotarised evidence, local counsel, standing as registrant or exclusive licenseeInjunction, damages and destruction of infringing goods

The 2026 Trademark Law strengthens the backdrop: Article 75 formalises two-way referral between administrative enforcement and criminal authorities; Article 76 lets enforcement bodies preserve evidence at risk of being lost; Article 77 expressly includes reasonable costs of stopping infringement in damages.

Customs Recordal: The Highest-Leverage Step After Registration

Customs protection has two modes. Without a recordal, Customs generally acts only on a specific application supported by evidence — which requires you to know about a shipment in advance. With a recordal, Customs can suspend clearance of suspect goods on its own initiative and notify the rights holder. Recordal is the precondition for that active mode.

ItemRule
DecisionWithin 30 working days of receiving a complete application
Validity10 years from approval; if the trademark's remaining term is shorter, the recordal follows the trademark term
RenewalApply in the 6 months before expiry; decision within 10 working days
ChangesApply to amend the recordal within 30 working days of any change to the recorded particulars
Foreign rights holdersFile through a domestic office or a Chinese agent
FeesFee schedules and any suspension of fees are set by GACC — confirm the current position rather than relying on third-party summaries

A typical application covers the registration certificate and its status, rights-holder identity and authorisation, photos of genuine goods and packaging, details of legitimate goods (names, origin, ports, importers, exporters, features, price), and known infringer or suspect-shipment intelligence. Foreign-language documents need a Chinese translation. Keep the list of authorised manufacturers and importers current: if it goes stale, legitimate shipments can be delayed while a counterfeit clears.

Practical point: Customs protection is generally tied to the mark as recorded. Brands using a main mark, sub-brands and defensive marks often need separate recordals for each, and should check that the goods listed in the original trademark application actually cover the products being shipped.

Platform Takedowns: Fast, Reactive and Evidence-Driven

Major e-commerce and content platforms operate intellectual property protection systems. Enrolment requires proof of rights — in practice a CNIPA registration certificate or a recorded licence. Once enrolled, complaints are assessed quickly and often by systems rather than lawyers, so the quality of the submission determines the outcome.

  • Identify the specific listing by URL and product ID, not by describing the seller generally.
  • State the registration number and attach the certificate.
  • Name the precise infringement basis: identical mark, counterfeit goods, unauthorised product imagery or copy, or a false claim of authorised-dealer status.
  • Attach annotated comparison evidence: listing screenshots against genuine product and packaging.
  • Expect counter-notifications and repeat sellers under new store names; sustained enforcement is a programme, not a one-off cleanup.
  • Document who holds complaint authority when a distributor or agency operates the store, so action can be taken in the brand's own name.

Inaccurate or abusive complaints can be penalised by the platforms. Keep the evidence file and the escalation rules in one place, alongside the use-evidence archive — the same dated screenshots and sales records serve both purposes.

Choosing a Route: A Decision Table

SituationFirst moveThen
Counterfeit listings appear on one platformPlatform complaint with a complete evidence packEscalate to AMR if the seller reappears repeatedly
Suspect goods are being exported from a factoryCustoms recordal plus AMR action at sourceCivil claim if the volumes justify damages
A distributor keeps selling after terminationAMR complaint + platform takedowns; check licence recordal statusLitigation for contract and infringement claims
Large-scale, organised counterfeitingNotarised evidence buy, then civil action with preservationCriminal referral through the administrative-criminal interface (Art. 75)

The common failure is treating these as alternatives. In practice they are sequential: monitoring finds the problem, recordal and evidence make action possible, platform complaints remove the visible listings, and administrative or court action changes the infringer's economics.

Sources and Caveats

Primary sources: Articles 75, 76 and 77 of the Trademark Law of the PRC (2026 Revision) (CNIPA, 26 June 2026); CNIPA Main Contents of the Revision (10 July 2026); official and government-published guidance on intellectual property Customs recordal (30-working-day decision, 10-year validity, 6-month renewal window, 30-working-day change window). Platform complaint mechanics and fee schedules are operational practice and change frequently — verify against each platform's current IP portal and GACC announcements before filing. This is general information, not legal advice.
